analysisDescription: Not as strighforward as I initially thought, since the more I thought about it, the more I realised that the way most people play Factorio, is just one of the ways one can play the game. And some interactions had me questioning my answers such as the interactions between players who are working on completely separate parts of a factory, but towards a common goal.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can play at the same time on the same game world and interact.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: There is a text chat, however the game does not incentivize or discourage it's use.

dimension.title: Agnostic
dimension.description: When Agnostic, the game is neutral to player communication, it does not incentivise nor it places any restrictions. It is the only communication design that does not promote cooperation.

dimensionExamples.example: There is a in-game text chat where besides typing, one can also embed small icons of in-game items.

dimension.title: Text Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using text

dimensionExamples.example: The players can host a game world as a server, and invite their friends to join.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: The main goal the game has is shared between all players in a server, that is: launching a rocket.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: The personal objectives of each player can differ, such as building a specific item processing plant, but in the end, they all affect each other when their resources are joined.

dimension.title: Intertwined
dimension.description: Intertwined goals determine individual objectives assigned to different players that, in some way, are dependent on each other. The dependency may be uni- or bidirectional. If the dependency is bidirectional, goals are interdependent.

dimensionExamples.example: The progression of players is tied to the game world (or server), and can be seen through the things that are build, the territory conquered, and especially with the technologies that are researched. All these are shared among players in a server.

dimension.title: Server
dimension.description: Server progression is defined by the existence of persistent mutable worlds that a number of players share. The action of players (i.e. collaborating or not) can impact the overall progression/evolution of the game world, affecting others.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player controls a single Engineer.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can also gain shared control over certain moving parts of the factory, such as the contruction/logistic bot network, or the automated train system.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared applies when input from multiple players directly translates to the actions of one playable entity

dimensionExamples.example: Each playable character is an engineer with the same capabilities.

dimension.title: Arbitrary
dimension.description: Arbitrary means that all player entities are equal in their ability to act upon the world. If a selection exists, it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimensionExamples.example: Although the research upgrades are pre-defined, the order in which the players choose to pursue them, and which ones to take advantage of are up to the player.

dimension.title: Customisable
dimension.description: Customisable encompasses all games with upgrades, levelling systems, and others that give players the ability to create and modify their representation throughout the game.

dimensionExamples.example: Formally there is no relationship between players, but they can join forces in order to progress in the game.

dimension.title: Allies
dimension.description: Allies, when players are part of a shared faction/race etc, which causes players to have special gameplay mechanics between each other.

dimensionExamples.example: All players share the same game world.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: Each players has a diferent view point from the POV of the their character, although spectating other players and looking throught the map are also possible.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: There are no explicit roles, each player does whatever tasks they feel like or were decided among the players.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimensionExamples.example: If two players build parts of a factory on the same server, but at diferent times so they never meet, they can still be collaborating.

dimension.title: Asynchronous Collaboration
dimension.description: In asynchronous collaboration, players are able to play at different times and still collaborate.

dimensionExamples.example: The game world does not scale its difficulty according to the number of players. Inclusively some of the harder presets/difficulties and almost impossible alone.

dimension.title: Fixed Difficulty
dimension.description: Fixed Difficulty, when games purposefully do not adapt the difficulty to player count, making some challenges near impossible without more players collaborating. While some players can take it as a challenge to complete on their own, others can rely on their fellow players to lighten up the challenge.

dimensionExamples.example: One player who is much more knowledgeable can build everything necessary to beat the game, while the other players simply "piggy-back"

dimension.title: Piggy-Backing
dimension.description: Piggy-Backing refers to a specific mechanic, where one player's performance can be leveraged for others to bypass challenges.

dimensionExamples.example: The factories themselves are shared among all players in the game world.

dimension.title: Interactables
dimension.description: Interactables refer to virtual objects and non-player characters/entities within the environment that respond to players’ actions. Interactables can be moved, shaped, or activated (e.g., a cannon that shoots when the player interacts with it). In some cases, interactables are also consumable (e.g., food in Overcooked is transported and modified as an interactable, but also consumed to complete the recipes). Interactables are shared when their state and attributes can be affected by more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Space is an important resource when building or expanding factories in this game, and players need to share it.

dimension.title: Space
dimension.description: Space is also a resource as it defines the various places in the environment that a player can occupy and interact with. Space is shared when its utilisation is affected or constrained by others' presence or by others’ actions.
